When the servants had set the meal ready before them, and they themselves had refreshed themselves with warm baths, gladly they pleased their hearts with food and drink. And after that Aeetes asked the sons of his daughter, addressing them with these encouraging words: "Sons of my child and of Phrixus, whom above all strangers I honoured in my halls, how have you come back to Aea? Did some calamity break your course midway as you sped? You did not heed me when I warned you of the boundless measure of the way. For I knew it once, whirled in the chariot of my father Helios, when he was bringing my sister Circe into the western land, and we came to the shore of the Tyrrhenian mainland, where even now she dwells, very far away from the Colchian land. But what pleasure is there in words? Tell me clearly what has befallen you, and who are these men that follow you, and where you stepped from your hollow ship."

As he questioned thus, before his brothers Argus, fearing for the company of Aeson's son, spoke gently, since he was the elder: "Aeetes, that ship the gusty storms scattered at once; and as we crouched upon the timbers the wave cast us up onto the dry land of the island of Enyalius in the murky night; and some god saved us. For even the birds of Ares that before now haunted that desolate island—not even those did we find. But these men had driven them away, going ashore from their ship the day before; and the will of Zeus, pitying us, kept them there, or else some fate, since at once they gave us food enough and clothing, hearing the glorious name of Phrixus and of yourself; for they are journeying to your city. And if you wish to know their need, I will not hide it from you. A certain king, eager to drive this man far from his country and his possessions, because in valour he was preeminent among all the sons of Aeolus, sends him here to make this impossible journey; and he declares that the Aeolids' race shall not escape the heart-grieving wrath of relentless Zeus, nor his anger, nor the unendurable pollution and the penalty for Phrixus, until the fleece comes to Hellas. And Pallas Athena built the ship, not such a one as the ships are among the Colchian men, the worst of which we chanced upon. For utterly the raging water and the wind tore it apart; but the other holds fast in its bolts, even if all the storms bear down upon it. And it runs as fast before the wind as when the men themselves press it on unceasingly with their hands at the oars. Having gathered into it the best of the heroes of all Achaea, he has come to your city, having wandered through many cities and seas of the dread brine, in the hope you will grant him the fleece. But as you see fit, so it shall be; for he does not come to use force; he is eager to render you a worthy recompense for the gift, since he has heard from me of those great foes, the Sauromatae, whom he will subdue beneath your sceptre. And if you wish indeed to know the names and lineage, who they are, I will tell you each thing. This man, for whose sake the others were gathered from Hellas, they call Jason, son of Aeson, son of Cretheus. And if he is truly of the stock of Cretheus himself, then he would be a kinsman of ours on the father's side. For both Cretheus and Athamas were sons of Aeolus; and Phrixus in turn was the son of Athamas the son of Aeolus. And this man, if you have heard of any offspring of Helios, you behold to be Augeias; and this is Telamon, sprung from most glorious Aeacus; and Zeus himself begot Aeacus. And so too all the rest, all the comrades who follow, are sons and grandsons of the immortals."

Such things Argus told; but the king's spirit swelled with anger as he listened; and high his mind soared in his wrath. And he spoke in indignation; and he was most enraged with the sons of Chalciope; for on their account, he supposed, the strangers had come; and his eyes flashed beneath his brows in his fury: "Out of my sight at once, you villains, go back with your tricks out of the land, before someone sees a baleful fleece and a Phrixus! Joining at once from Hellas, not for the fleece but for my sceptre and royal honour, you come here. If you had not first touched my table, truly I would have cut out your tongues and hewn off both your hands and sent you forth with only your feet, that you might be restrained from setting out even hereafter, seeing what lies too you have invented against the blessed gods."

So he spoke in his anger; and greatly the heart of Aeacus' son swelled within from the depths; and his spirit longed to speak a deadly word in answer face to face; but Aeson's son restrained him; for he himself first answered with soft words: "Aeetes, bear with this expedition of mine. For not at all do we come to your city and halls as you perhaps suppose, nor of our own desire. Who would willingly endure to cross so great a swell of sea for another's possession? But a divinity and the cruel command of a wicked king has stirred me. Grant a favour to your suppliants; and through all Hellas I will bear your divine renown; and indeed we are already ready to pay you swift recompense in war, whether it is the Sauromatae you desire, or some other people you would subdue beneath your sceptre."

So he spoke, fawning with gentle voice; but the other's spirit seethed within his breast with a twofold purpose, whether to set upon them and slay them there outright, or to make trial of their strength. This seemed to him the better as he pondered; and he answered him with these words: "Stranger, why recount each thing at length? For if you are truly the race of gods, or otherwise have come no worse than I against another's goods, I will give you the golden fleece to take, if you wish, when you have been tried. For toward brave men I grudge nothing, such as you tell me is he who rules in Hellas. And the trial of your courage and strength shall be a contest, which I myself accomplish with my hands, deadly though it is. Two bulls of bronze feet range the plain of Ares, breathing flame from their mouths; these I yoke and drive over the stubborn fallow of Ares, four acres, and quickly cutting it to the boundary with the plough I cast into the furrows not the seed of Demeter's grain, but the teeth of a dread serpent, which grow into the bodies of armed men. These then, slaying them on the spot, I cut down with my spear as they rise against me on every side. At dawn I yoke the oxen, and at the hour of evening I cease from the harvest. And you, if you accomplish these things thus, on the same day shall carry off this fleece to the king's house; but before that I will not give it, do not hope for it. For indeed it is unseemly that a man who is born noble should yield to a meaner man."

So he spoke; and Jason, fixing his eyes upon the ground before his feet, sat just so, speechless, helpless in his trouble. For a long time he turned the plan over, and could in no way take it up boldly, since the deed appeared great. At last, answering, he addressed him with cunning words: "Aeetes, with full justice you hold me hard pressed. Therefore I too will dare this contest, overweening as it is, even if it is my fate to die. For no other thing more dreadful will lie upon men than harsh necessity, which has compelled me to come even here at a king's bidding."

So he spoke, smitten with helplessness; but the other addressed him in his distress with terrible words: "Go now to the company, since you are eager for the labour; but if you should shrink from lifting the yoke upon the oxen, or draw back from the deadly harvest, then all these things shall be my care, so that another man too may shudder to go after a better man."

So he spoke openly; and Jason rose from his seat, and Augeias and Telamon at once; and Argus followed, alone, for he had signed midway to his brothers to remain there yet; and they went out of the hall. And wondrously among them all shone the son of Aeson in beauty and grace; and upon him the maiden, casting a sidelong glance past her bright veil, gazed, her heart smouldering with anguish; and her mind like a dream crept hovering after him as he went.

And so they went out of the house, sorrowing. And Chalciope, guarding herself against Aeetes' wrath, went quickly to her chamber with her sons. And Medea likewise withdrew; and much in her heart she pondered, all that the Loves stir one to care for. And still before her eyes all things appeared, himself, what he was like, and in what robes he was clad, what he said, how he sat upon his seat, how toward the door he went; nor did she think, in her brooding, that any other man was such as he; and ever in her ears there rang his voice and the honey-sweet words that he had spoken. And she trembled for him, lest the bulls or Aeetes himself should destroy him; and she mourned as though he were already quite dead, and down her tender cheeks a tear ran from most piteous pity in her cares; and softly weeping she shrilly lifted up her voice: "Why does this grief possess me, wretched as I am? Whether he, of all the heroes, is to perish the foremost, or whether the worse, let him be gone. And yet would that he might escape unharmed. Yes, lady goddess, daughter of Perses, may this come to pass, that he return home escaping his doom; but if it is his fate to be slain by the bulls, may he learn this first, that I take no pleasure in his cruel ruin."
So the maiden was distraught in mind with her cares.

But they, when they had passed beyond the people and the city by the road by which they had come up from the plain, then Argus addressed Jason with these words: "Aeson's son, you will scorn the counsel that I shall tell; but it is not fitting to give up the trial in our distress. You have yourself heard from me before of a certain maiden who works charms by the counsels of Hecate, daughter of Perses. If we could win her over, I think there would be no more fear for you in the contest, of being overcome; but I am terribly afraid that my mother will not undertake this for me. Nevertheless I will go back again to entreat her, since a common ruin hangs over us all."

So he spoke with good will; and Jason answered him with these words: "Good friend, if this is pleasing to you, I do not object. Go then, and with shrewd words stir your mother with entreaty; yet feeble is the hope that has arisen for us, when we entrust our homecoming to women."

So he spoke; and quickly they reached the marsh again. But their comrades joyfully questioned them, when they saw them present; and to them Aeson's son spoke this word in grief: "Friends, the heart of pitiless Aeetes is set against us outright in anger; for each thing has no end either for me or for you if you should ask. He said that two bulls of bronze feet range the plain of Ares, breathing flame from their mouths. And on these he bade me plough up four acres of fallow; and he will give from a serpent's jaws a seed that sends up earthborn men in armour of bronze; and on that same day I must slay them. This—since there was no other better thing to devise—I undertook outright."

So he spoke; and to all the contest seemed impossible, and long in silence and speechless they looked at one another, downcast with calamity and helplessness; but at last Peleus spoke boldly among all the chieftains: "It is time to take counsel what we shall do. Yet I do not think there is so much profit in counsel as in the strength of our hands. If now you yourself purpose to yoke the bulls of Aeetes, hero, son of Aeson, and are eager for the labour, then truly, keeping your promise, you may make ready; but if your spirit does not trust altogether in its own valour, neither hasten yourself, nor look about to any other of these men sitting by. For I will not hold back, since death will be the worst of pains."

So spoke Aeacus' son; and Telamon's spirit was stirred; and eagerly he sprang up swiftly; and third Idas rose, mighty in pride, and upon them the sons of Tyndareus; and with them too the son of Oeneus, counted among grown men, though not so much as the down was sprouting on his cheeks; with such strength was his spirit lifted. But the others yielded and kept silence. And straightway Argus spoke this word to them who longed for the contest: "Friends, truly this is our last resort. But I think there will be some timely help for you from my mother. Therefore, eager as you are, restrain yourselves in the ship a little while yet, as before, since even to hold back is after all better than to seize a wretched doom by recklessness. A certain maiden is reared in the halls of Aeetes, whom the goddess Hecate taught beyond all others to handle drugs, all that the mainland and the brimming water bring forth. With these even the breath of unwearying fire is softened, and she stays at once the rivers that flow loud-roaring, and binds the stars and the paths of the sacred moon. Of her we bethought ourselves as we came hither along the path from the hall, whether she, being our mother's sister, might be able to persuade our mother to aid us in the contest. And if this is pleasing to you too, then I will go this very day back to the house of Aeetes to make trial; and perhaps with some god's help I shall succeed."

So he spoke; and the gods in their kindness gave them a sign. A trembling dove, fleeing the might of a hawk, fell from on high in terror into the lap of Aeson's son; and the hawk dashed itself upon the ship's stern. And quickly Mopsus spoke this word of prophecy among them all: "For you, friends, this sign is wrought by the will of the gods; nor is there any better way to interpret it, than to approach the maiden with words, plying her with every device. And I think she will not refuse, if truly Phineus said that our homecoming would lie with the goddess Cypris. The gentle bird of hers escaped its doom; and as my heart within my breast forebodes from this omen, so may it come to pass. But, friends, calling on Cytherea to aid us, now obey the counsels of Argus."

So he spoke; and the young men approved, remembering the charges of Phineus. Only Idas, son of Aphareus, leapt up, terribly indignant, and cried out with a great voice: "Alas, have we come here as fellow-voyagers with women, who call on Cypris to be our helper, and no longer on the great might of Enyalius? And looking to doves and hawks, do you hold back from the contest? Be gone, and let no warlike deeds be your concern, but to beguile feeble maidens with prayers!"

So he spoke in his eagerness; and many of the comrades murmured low, yet none spoke a word against him to his face. And in his anger he then sat down; and Jason at once, rousing their resolve, spoke his mind thus: "Let Argus set out from the ship, since this is pleasing to all; but we ourselves will now openly make fast our cables to the shore from the river. For surely it is fitting no longer to hide cowering from the war-cry."

So he spoke; and at once he sent him off to go quickly back into the city; and they, drawing up the anchor-stones of the ship at the bidding of Aeson's son, rowed it a little out of the marsh and beached it on the dry land.

But straightway Aeetes held an assembly of the Colchians apart from his own house, where also before they used to sit, devising unbearable treacheries and woes for the Minyae. He vowed that, as soon as the bulls had torn in pieces the man who had undertaken to accomplish the heavy contest, he would tear up the thicket above the shaggy hill and burn the ship with all its crew, that they might spew out their grievous insolence, plotting their overweening deeds. For he said he would never have received the Aeolid Phrixus as a guest in his halls, however much he needed it, Phrixus who excelled all strangers in gentleness and fear of the gods, had not Zeus himself sent from heaven Hermes as messenger, that he might meet with a kindly host; much less would robbers coming into his land be long unpunished, men whose care it is to lay their hands upon the goods of strangers, and to contrive secret treacheries, and to ravage the steadings of herdsmen with ill-sounding raids. And besides he said that the sons of Phrixus would pay him a fitting recompense, since they had come back in company with evildoing men, that they might drive him from his honour and his sceptre, heedless of him; even as once a baleful oracle he had heard from his father Helios, that he must avoid the cunning treachery and the plans of his own offspring and their manifold mischief; therefore he was sending them, eager as they were, to the Achaean land at their father's bidding, a long journey. And of his daughters he had not the least fear, that they might devise some hateful plot, nor of his son Apsyrtus; but in the race of Chalciope these woes were appointed to be. And he declared his unbearable purposes to the people in his wrath; and greatly he threatened to guard the ship and the men themselves, that none might escape from ruin.

Meanwhile, going to the house of Aeetes, Argus tried to persuade his mother with all manner of words to entreat Medea to help them; and she herself had already thought of this; but fear held back her spirit, lest perhaps she should plead in vain and beyond what was fated, since the girl was dismayed by her father's deadly wrath, or lest, if she yielded to the prayers, the deeds should become clear and open.

But upon the maiden a deep sleep relieved her of her griefs as she lay back upon her bed. And straightway beguiling dreams, such as come to one in distress, baneful, kept troubling her. She thought the stranger had taken up the contest, not at all eager to carry off the ram's fleece, nor for the sake of that had he come to the city of Aeetes, but that he might lead her to his own home as his wedded wife; and she dreamed that she herself about the bulls was contending, accomplishing it very easily; but that her own parents made light of the promise, because they had not bidden the girl to yoke the bulls, but him himself; and from this there arose a quarrel of dispute between her father and the strangers; and to her both gave it over to decide as she should choose in her own mind. And she suddenly, scorning her parents, chose the stranger; and unspeakable grief seized them, and they cried out in anger; and with the cry sleep released her. Trembling she started up in fear, and round about the walls of the chamber she looked; and hardly did she gather her spirit back into her breast as before, and lifted up a wailing voice: "Wretched that I am, how the heavy dreams have frightened me! I fear lest this journey of the heroes bring some great evil. My heart is in a flutter for the stranger. Let him woo some Achaean girl far away among his own people; but let maidenhood and my parents' house be my concern. Yet, putting on a shameless heart, no longer apart from my sister will I make trial, whether she may ask me to help in the contest, grieving for her sons; that would quench the bitter pain in my heart."

She spoke, and rose and opened the doors of her chamber, barefoot, in a single garment; and indeed she longed to go to her sister, and she crossed the threshold of the court. But long she stayed there in the porch of her chamber, held back by shame; and she turned back again behind her, wheeling about; and from within she came out again, and shrank back inside; her feet bore her this way and that to no purpose; whenever she set out, shame held her back within; and held back by shame, bold desire urged her on. Three times she made the attempt, three times she held back; the fourth time she fell prone upon her bed, writhing. As when a bride mourns in her chamber her vigorous husband, to whom her brothers and parents had given her, nor does she yet mingle with all her handmaids out of modesty and discretion, but sits grieving in a corner; and some doom has destroyed him, before the two could take delight in each other's love; and she, burning within, weeps in silence, looking on her widowed bed, lest the women mock her with their jeers; like her Medea lamented. And as she wept, one of the handmaids, coming up midway, suddenly noticed her, one who was her young attendant; and at once she told Chalciope; and she among her sons sat planning how to win over her sister. But even so she did not disbelieve, when she heard from the handmaid the unlooked-for word; and amazed she rushed straight from chamber to chamber, where the girl lay grieving, and had torn her cheeks on either side; and when she saw her eyes defiled with tears, she spoke to her: "Ah me, Medea, why do you shed these tears? What has befallen you? What dread grief has come upon your heart? Has some heaven-sent sickness coursed through your limbs, or have you learned of some deadly threat from our father against me and my sons? Would that I might look upon neither this house of my parents, nor the city, but dwell at the ends of the earth, where not even the name of the Colchians is known."

So she spoke; and the girl's cheeks flushed; and long did maidenly shame keep her back from answering, eager though she was. Now the word would rise to the very tip of her tongue, now it flew back down within her breast. Often it surged to her lovely lips to be told; but no further came the sound; at last she spoke thus, with guile; for bold Loves pressed hard upon her: "Chalciope, my heart is in a flutter for your sons, lest my father destroy them at once together with the stranger men. Such things, sinking into brief sleep just now, I saw in baleful dreams, which may some god render of no effect, nor may you take grievous sorrow for your sons."

So she spoke, making trial of her sister, whether she would first entreat her to aid her children. But unbearable anguish overwhelmed her sister's spirit with terror at what she heard; and she answered thus with words: "I too came after all these things, pondering, whether you might devise and contrive some help with me. But swear by Earth and Heaven that what I tell you you will keep in your heart, and be a fellow-worker with me. I beseech you by the blessed gods, and by yourself and your parents, not to see them destroyed by an evil doom, wretchedly; or else may I, dying together with my dear sons, become afterward a hateful Fury upon you from Hades."

So she spoke, and at once a flood of tears poured forth; and below she clasped her sister's knees with both her hands, and let her head fall upon her lap. Then a piteous wailing they raised, each over the other; and a thin moaning rose through the house of the two grieving in their sorrows. And Medea first addressed her in distress: "Strange one, what remedy can I work for you, who speak of curses and hateful Furies? Would that it lay firmly in my power to save your sons. Let the dread oath of the Colchians be my witness, by which you yourself bid me swear, great Heaven, and Earth below, mother of the gods, that with all the strength that is in me I will not fail you, if you ask things that can be done."

She spoke; and Chalciope answered her with these words: "Could you not then, for the stranger, since he too is in need, devise some trick or some plan for the contest, for my sons' sake? And from him comes Argus, urging me to make trial of your aid; midway I left him in the house when I came here."

So she spoke; and within the heart of Medea leapt with joy, and her fair skin flushed all at once, and a mist came over her as she was warmed with gladness, and she spoke this word: "Chalciope, as is dear and delightful to you both, so will I do. For may the dawn not shine in my eyes, nor may you look on me alive much longer, if I hold anything dearer than your life, or than your sons, who are indeed my brothers, dear kinsmen and of my own age. And so too I declare myself to be your sister and your child, since you reared me at your breast as one of them, a little child, as I ever heard from my mother. But go, hide my favour in silence, that I may escape my parents' notice while I prepare the promise; and at dawn I will bring to the temple of Hecate charms to enchant the bulls."

So she went again out of the chamber, and told her sons of their aunt's help. But again shame and hateful fear seized her, left alone, to be contriving such things against her father, on a man's behalf.

Night then drew darkness over the earth; and on the sea the sailors looked from their ships toward the Bear and the stars of Orion; and now the wayfarer and the gatekeeper longed for sleep; and some mother of dead children a deep slumber enfolded; nor was there any more barking of dogs through the city, nor ringing sound; silence held the darkening gloom. But by no means did sweet sleep seize Medea. For many cares wakened her in her longing for Aeson's son, fearing the mighty strength of the bulls, by which he was destined to perish by an unseemly fate on the plain of Ares. And fast her heart throbbed within her breast, as when a sunbeam quivers within a house, darting up from water just now poured into a cauldron or perhaps into a pail; and here and there in the swift eddy it is shaken as it leaps; so too within her breast the girl's heart quivered. And a tear of pity flowed from her eyes; and within anguish ever tormented her, smouldering through her flesh, about the fine sinews and beneath the lowest nape of the head, where the most grievous pain sinks in, whenever the unwearying Loves cast their sorrows upon the heart. And she said to herself, now that she would give the charms to enchant the bulls, now that she would not; and that she herself would perish too; and then again that she would neither die herself, nor give the charms, but would just endure her ruin in quiet. Then sitting down she pondered, and spoke aloud: "Wretched that I am, here am I, between one evil and another. On every side my wits are helpless; nor is there any defence against my pain; but it burns me steadily, without ceasing. Would that I had been slain before by the swift arrows of Artemis, before I had set eyes on him, before the sons of Chalciope had come to the Achaean land. Them some god or some Fury brought hither from there, much-lamented sorrows for us. Let him perish in the contest, if it is his fate to die on the plain. For how could I prepare the charms unnoticed by my parents? What story shall I tell? What trick, what cunning device shall there be for my aid? Shall I greet him alone, apart from his comrades, when I see him? Ill-starred that I am! I do not hope, even if he should die, to find rest from my griefs; then evil would come to me, when he is bereft of life. Away with shame, away with my glory! And he, saved by my will, unharmed, where it pleases his heart, there let him go. But I, on the very day he accomplishes the contest, let me die, either fastening a noose about my throat to the roof-beam, or tasting drugs that destroy the spirit. Yet even so, when I am dead, they will cast scoffs at me hereafter; and far off the whole city will cry aloud my doom; and the Colchian women, bearing me about on their lips, this way and that, will mock me shamefully— the girl who, caring so for a foreign man, died, who disgraced her house and her parents, yielding to wantonness. What shame will not be mine? Ah me, for my ruin! Truly it would be far better this very night to leave my life in my chamber by an unlooked-for doom, escaping all evil reproaches, before I accomplish these shameful and unspeakable deeds."

She spoke, and went to fetch a casket, in which lay many drugs, some healing, some destroying. And setting it upon her knees she wept; and she drenched her bosom unceasingly with tears, which flowed unstanched just so, as she bitterly bewailed her own doom. And she longed to choose out the drugs that destroy the spirit, that she might taste them. And now she was loosing the fastenings of the casket, eager to take them out, ill-fated one. But suddenly a deadly dread of hateful Hades came over her heart. And long she was held in speechlessness, and round about her all the heart-pleasing cares of life appeared. She remembered the delights, all that there are among the living; she remembered her glad companions, such as a girl knows; and the sun grew sweeter for her to behold than before, if in truth her mind reached after each thing. And she set the casket back again from her knees, turned about by the promptings of Hera, and no longer debated her plans this way and that; but she longed for dawn to appear at once, that she might give him the enchanting charms by agreement, and meet him face to face. And often she loosed the bolts of her doors, watching for the gleam; and gladly to her the light shed by the Dawn-born, and people stirred throughout the city.

And she, when first she saw the dawn shining, the maiden, bound up with her hands her golden hair, which had hung loose and unkempt in her neglect, and cleansed her dry cheeks; and with ambrosial ointment she brightened her skin; and she put on a lovely robe, fitted with well-curved clasps; and over her divine head she threw a silvery veil. And there in the house, moving about, she trod the floor, forgetting her griefs that lay before her feet, the wondrous ones, and others that were to grow hereafter. And she called to her handmaids, who in all were twelve, who lodged in the porch of her fragrant chamber, her companions, not yet sharing the bed with men, to yoke the mules in haste to the chariot, to carry her to the lovely temple of Hecate. Then the handmaids made ready the chariot; and she meanwhile took out from the hollow casket a drug which they say is called the drug of Prometheus. If a man, having appeased the only-begotten maiden with nightly sacrifice, should anoint his body with it, then truly he could neither be cut by strokes of bronze, nor would he yield to blazing fire; but in valour too he would be the better that day, alike in might. It first sprang up when the flesh-eating eagle let drip to the ground on the Caucasian crags the bloody ichor of suffering Prometheus. And its flower appeared a cubit high above, in colour like the Corycian crocus, raised on twin stalks; but in the earth the root was like flesh newly cut. The dark juice of it, like the black sap of a mountain oak, she had gathered in a Caspian shell to make her charm, having bathed seven times in ever-flowing streams, and seven times having called on Brimo, nurse of youth, Brimo, night-wanderer, of the underworld, queen of the dead, in the murky night, in dark garments. And with a bellowing the dark earth shook beneath as the Titan root was cut; and groaned himself the son of Iapetus, his spirit distracted with pain. This she drew forth and set in a fragrant band, which was tied about her ambrosial breast. And going out of doors she stepped upon the swift chariot; and with her two handmaids mounted on either side. And she herself took the reins and the well-made whip in her right hand, and drove through the city; and the other handmaids, holding to the chariot-frame behind, ran along the broad highway; and their thin tunics they lifted up to the white of the knee. And as by the warm waters of Parthenius, or having bathed in the river Amnisus, Leto's daughter, standing on her golden chariot, drives with her swift deer over the hills, coming from afar to a rich-savoured hecatomb; and with her follow the nymphs, her attendants, gathered some at the very spring of Amnisus, and others about the groves and the many-fountained peaks; and round about the beasts fawn and whimper, cowering as she goes; so they sped through the city; and on either side the people gave way, avoiding the eyes of the royal maiden. But when she had left the well-built streets of the city, and reached the temple, driving across the plains, then she stepped down eagerly there from the swift-wheeled chariot, and spoke thus among her handmaids: "Friends, truly I have greatly erred, and did not consider that I ought not to go among foreign men, who roam over our land. The whole city is smitten with helplessness; and so none of those women have come up here who before gathered here day by day. But since we have come, and no one else approaches, come, let us satisfy our hearts to the full with sweet song, and gathering the lovely flowers of the soft grass, then at the same hour we will return. And you shall come home with many gifts this day, if you will agree with me in this desire. For Argus turns me with his words, and so too does Chalciope; but keep in your minds, hearing this in silence from me, that no word may reach my father's ears. They bid me, taking gifts, to rescue the stranger who undertook the contest with the bulls from his deadly trials. But I approved the plan, and I bid him come into my sight alone, apart from his comrades, that we may divide the gifts among ourselves, if he brings and gives them, and may give him in turn a worse drug. But stand apart from me when he comes."

So she spoke; and the cunning plan pleased them all. And straightway, drawing Aeson's son alone from his comrades, Argus, when now he heard from his brothers that she had gone in the morning to the holy temple of Hecate, led him across the plain; and with them went Mopsus, son of Ampycus, skilled to interpret the birds that appeared, and skilled to give good counsel to those who set out.

Never yet was there such a man among men of former times, neither of those who are the race of Zeus himself, nor of those who sprang from the blood of the other immortals, as Jason was made that day by the wife of Zeus, both to look upon face to face, and to speak with. And gazing on him his very comrades marvelled, shining with grace; and the son of Ampycus rejoiced in the journey, already foreseeing each thing.

There is, along the path of the plain near the temple, a poplar luxuriant with countless leaves, on which the chattering crows often roosted. One of them midway, flapping her wings high on the topmost boughs, rebuked the counsels of Hera: "A glory-less seer is this, who does not even know in his mind what children know, that neither pleasant nor lovely word will a maiden speak to a youth, while strangers follow at his side. Be gone, foul-prophesying, ill-counselling seer! Neither Cypris nor the gentle loving Loves breathe upon you."

So she spoke in reproach; and Mopsus smiled, hearing the heaven-sent voice of the bird, and spoke thus: "Go you to the temple of the goddess, where you will find the girl, son of Aeson; and very kindly you will meet her by the counsels of Cypris, who shall be your fellow-worker in the contest, as before Phineus the son of Agenor foretold. But we two, Argus and I, will withdraw, awaiting you when you come, in this very place; and you, alone, entreat her, winning her over with shrewd words."
He spoke with full wisdom; and both approved nearby.

Nor indeed did the heart of Medea turn to think of other things, for all her singing; and no song that she played at, none pleased her long to amuse herself with. But helpless she kept breaking off, nor ever held her eyes steady among the throng of her handmaids; but toward the paths she kept gazing far off, turning aside her cheek. And often her heart broke within her breast, whenever she fancied the sound of a footstep or of the wind passing by. But not long after he appeared to her in her longing, springing up on high like Sirius from Ocean, who indeed rises fair and clear to behold, but brings unspeakable woe upon the flocks; so to her there came, fair to look upon, the son of Aeson, but by his appearing he woke the pain of ill-starred love. And her heart fell from her breast, and her eyes grew dim of themselves; and a warm flush seized her cheeks. Her knees she had no strength to lift, either backward or forward, but beneath her her feet were fixed fast. And meanwhile all her handmaids had withdrawn apart from them. And the two stood speechless and without voice facing each other, like oaks, or like tall pines, which stand rooted side by side quietly in the mountains, in a windless calm; but afterward again, by a gust of wind stirred, they murmur endlessly; so these two were destined to speak much under the breath of Love.

And Aeson's son knew that she had fallen into love-stricken distress by heaven's decree, and spoke this soothing word: "Why, maiden, do you so dread me, who am alone? I am not, like other vainglorious men there are, not even when I dwelt in my own country was I before. So do not be too shy of me, girl, either to ask whatever you wish, or to say anything. But since we have come together with kindly intent, in a holy place, where it is not lawful to do wrong, speak openly and ask; nor with pleasant words beguile me, since at the first you promised to your sister to give me welcome charms. I beseech you by Hecate herself and by your parents and by Zeus, who holds out his hand over strangers and suppliants; both as suppliant and stranger I come hither to you, entreating you in bitter necessity. For without you I shall not be superior in the grievous contest. And to you I would render thanks hereafter for your aid, as is right, as befits those who dwell far apart, making your name and fair renown; and so too the other heroes will glorify you, returning to Hellas, and the wives of heroes and their mothers, who perhaps already sit on the shores and lament for us; their grievous pains you might scatter. Once too Theseus was delivered from his evil trials by the maiden, daughter of Minos, kindly-minded Ariadne, whom Pasiphae, daughter of Helios, bore. But she, when Minos had lulled his wrath, sat with him in the ship and left her country; and her the immortals themselves loved, and as a sign for her in mid-air a crown of stars, which men call Ariadne's, wheels all night long among the heavenly constellations. So too for you there shall be thanks from the gods, if you save so great a company of noble men. For truly you seem from your form to be adorned with gentle courtesies."

So he spoke, glorifying her; and she, casting down her eyes to one side, smiled a nectarous smile; and her spirit melted within uplifted by his praise, and she looked up straight into his eyes; nor did she know what word to speak first, but longed to pour out all things at once together. And without restraint she drew forth from the fragrant band the charm; and he straightway received it gladly in his hands. And now she would even have drawn all her soul from her breast and given it him, rejoicing, at his desire; such love flashed its sweet flame from the golden head of Aeson's son; and it caught up the glances of her eyes; and her heart within grew warm, melting, as the dew melts about the roses, warmed by the morning beams. And the two now would fix their eyes upon the ground, abashed, now again would cast their glances upon each other, smiling with love beneath their bright brows. And at last, hardly, the girl addressed him thus: "Mark now, how I will devise aid for you. When at your coming my father gives into your hands from the serpent's jaws the deadly teeth to sow, then, watching for the dividing of midnight, having bathed in the streams of the unwearying river, alone, apart from the others, in dark garments, dig a round pit; and in it slay a ewe lamb, and lay it whole upon the fire, having heaped the pyre well over the pit itself. And propitiate the only-begotten Hecate, daughter of Perses, pouring from the cup the hive-labours of bees. And there, when you have remembered and appeased the goddess, draw back from the pyre; and let no sound, either of feet, move you to turn back behind, nor barking of dogs, lest by spoiling each thing you yourself come not duly to your comrades. And at dawn, having steeped this charm, like an ointment strip and anoint your body; and in it there will be boundless might and great strength, and you would say that you matched not men, but the immortal gods. And besides, let your spear too be sprinkled, and your shield, and your sword. Then the points of the earthborn men could not cut through you, nor the irresistible darting flame of the deadly bulls. Yet such you will not be for long, but for that one day; still, never withdraw from the contest. And I will tell you another help besides. At once, when you have yoked the strong bulls, and quickly with your hands and your valour have ploughed up all the stubborn fallow, and they, the Giants, now spring up along the furrows where the serpent's teeth are sown upon the dark clod, if you see many rising from the fallow, secretly cast among them a heavy stone; and over it they, like ravening dogs over their food, will slay one another; and you yourself hasten to rush into the fray. And the fleece, for that reason, to Hellas you shall carry far away from Aea; yet go nonetheless wherever you please, or wherever you are minded to go, when you have set out."

So she spoke, and in silence cast her eyes to the ground before her feet, and wet her divine cheek with warm tears, weeping, that he was to wander far away from her over the sea; and with a sorrowful word, face to face, again she addressed him, and took him by his right hand; for now shame had left her eyes: "Remember, if ever you come back home again, the name of Medea; and so I likewise, even when you are far away, will remember you. But tell me kindly this, where lie your halls, where now from here will you cross over the sea in your ship; will you come near to rich Orchomenus, or near the isle of Aeaea? And tell me of the maiden, whoever this is you named, the renowned daughter of Pasiphae, who is of one stock with my father."

So she spoke; and over him too the tears of the maiden brought stealing fell Love, and he answered thus: "Truly I think that neither by night nor ever by day shall I forget you, if I escape my doom, and if in truth I flee unscathed to Achaea, and if Aeetes sets no other worse contest before us. But if it pleases you to know of our country, I will tell it; for my heart too greatly bids me. There is a land ringed about by lofty mountains, rich in flocks and good pasture, where Prometheus, son of Iapetus, begot good Deucalion, who first made cities and built temples to the immortals, and first was king over men. The neighbouring peoples call that land Haemonia. In it is Iolcus, my city, and in it also many other cities are inhabited, where not even the name of the isle of Aeaea is heard. Yet Minyas they say, setting out, Aeolian Minyas, from there once founded the city of Orchomenus on the borders of the Cadmeans. But why do I tell you all these idle things, of our home and of far-famed Ariadne, daughter of Minos, by which glorious name they called that lovely maiden, of whom you ask me? Would that, as Minos then agreed with Theseus concerning her, so your father might be in friendship with us."

So he spoke, soothing her with gentle words. But the most grievous anguish stirred her heart, and in her sorrow she addressed him with a piercing word: "In Hellas perhaps this is well, to observe agreements. But Aeetes is not such a man among men as you said Minos was, the husband of Pasiphae; nor with Ariadne do I match myself; therefore do not speak of hospitality. But only do you remember me, when you reach Iolcus; and you I will remember, even against the will of my parents. And may there come to us from afar some rumour, or some messenger bird, when you have forgotten me; or may swift storms snatch me up over the sea from here to Iolcus and carry me, that I may bring reproaches before your eyes, and remind you that you escaped by my will. Would that I might then unannounced be a guest in your halls."

So she spoke, pouring piteous tears down her cheeks; and to her he answered insinuatingly: "Strange one, let the empty storms wander idly, and so too the messenger bird, since you speak vain things. But if you should come to those abodes and the land of Hellas, honoured and revered you will be among women and men; and they will tend you wholly as a goddess, because by your counsel their sons returned home, and by it again their brothers and kinsmen and stout husbands were saved enough from ruin. And our bridal bed in our wedded chamber you shall prepare; nor shall anything part us from our love, until death, appointed, enfolds us round."

So he spoke; and within her her spirit melted at his words; yet she shuddered to look upon the dread deeds before her. Poor wretch! Not long was she to refuse to dwell in Hellas. For thus Hera devised it, that Aeaean Medea might come, an evil to Pelias, to holy Iolcus, leaving her native land.

And now the handmaids, watching from afar, were grieved in silence; and the hour of the day was passing for the maiden to go back home to her mother. But she did not yet think of returning, for her spirit delighted both in his form and in his winning words, until at last Aeson's son, wary, spoke late: "It is time to depart, lest the light of the sun set first and overtake us, and some stranger notice each thing; but we will meet again, coming here."

So they two with gentle words made trial of each other thus far; and then again they parted. Jason went off rejoicing to his comrades and the ship; and she to her handmaids; and they came up to meet her all together; but she did not notice them as they thronged about her. For her soul had flown aloft among the clouds. And with feet that moved of themselves she stepped upon the swift chariot, and with one hand took the reins, and with the other the whip of cunning work, to drive the mules; and they toward the city sped hastening to the halls. And as she came Chalciope, grieving for her sons, questioned her; but she, helpless in her wavering, neither heard the words, nor was minded to answer her questioning. And she sat upon a low stool below her couch, leaning sideways, her cheek upon her left hand; and moist were her eyes within their lids, as she pondered what an evil deed she had shared by her counsel.

But Aeson's son, when he had mingled again with his comrades in the place where he had left them when he withdrew, set out to go with them, telling them each thing, to the throng of the heroes; and together they came near the ship. And they embraced him when they saw him, and questioned him. And he told them all of the girl's counsels, and showed the dread drug; but alone of his comrades Idas sat apart, gnawing his anger; while the rest, glad of heart, since the darkness of night now stayed them, took their ease about their own concerns. But at dawn they sent two men to go to Aeetes and ask for the seed, first warlike Telamon himself, and with him Aethalides, the renowned son of Hermes. And they went, nor did they make their journey in vain; for when they came the lord Aeetes gave them, for the contest, the harsh teeth of the Aonian dragon, which in Ogygian Thebes Cadmus, when he came seeking Europa, slew, where it kept guard over the spring of Ares; and there he settled, led by the cow which Apollo gave him by his oracles to be the guide of his way. These the Tritonian goddess drew from the jaws and gave to Aeetes as a gift, together with the slayer himself. And Cadmus, son of Agenor, sowing them over the Aonian plains, set up an earthborn people, all that were left of those reaped by the spear of Ares; and these Aeetes then gave to be carried to the ship readily, since he did not think Jason would accomplish the end of the contest, even if he should cast the yoke upon the oxen.

The sun was sinking far away beneath the dark earth in the west, beyond the farthest peaks of the Ethiopians; and Night laid the yoke upon her horses; and the heroes made ready their beds beside the cables. But Jason, as soon as the stars of the bright-shining Bear of Helice had declined, and the heaven became wholly calm, went off to a desolate place, like some stealthy thief, with all that he needed; for beforehand he had provided each thing by day: a ewe and milk Argus had brought from outside the flock, and the rest he took from the ship itself. But when he saw a place that was away from the tread of men, in the open under clear pure meadows, there first of all he bathed his tender body reverently in the divine river; and about him a cloak of dark hue he put on, which before Hypsipyle of Lemnos had given him, a memorial of their close love. Then digging a pit a cubit deep in the ground he heaped the billets, and over it cut the throat of the lamb, and stretched it duly above; and he kindled the logs, setting fire beneath, and poured mingled libations over it, calling on Brimo Hecate to aid him in the contest. And when he had called on her he went back again; and she, hearing, the dread goddess, came up from the uttermost depths to the sacrifice of Aeson's son; and round about her were wreathed terrible serpents amid oak-branches. And there flashed an endless gleam of torches; and about her the hounds of the underworld bayed with sharp barking. And all the meadows trembled along her path; and the marsh-nymphs and river-nymphs cried aloud, who circle round about that meadow of Phasis by Amarantus. And dread indeed seized Aeson's son; yet even so his feet bore him on, glancing back, until he reached his comrades as he went; and already over the snowy heights of Caucasus the early-born Dawn shed light as she rose.

And then Aeetes put on about his breast the stiff corselet, which Ares had given him, having slain Phlegraean Mimas with his own hands; and on his head he set a golden four-crested helmet, shining like the rounded radiance of the sun, when first it rises from Ocean. And he wielded his shield of many hides, and his spear, dread, irresistible; this no other man of the heroes could have withstood, since they had left Heracles far behind, who alone could have warred against it face to face. And nearby Phaethon held for him the well-made chariot of swift-footed horses to mount; and he himself mounted, and took the reins in his hands. And out of the city he drove along the broad highway, that he might be present at the contest; and with him a countless host poured forth. And as Poseidon goes to the Isthmian games, mounted in his chariot, or to Taenarus, or to the water of Lerna, or through the grove of Hyantian Onchestus, and goes thereafter with his horses to Calaureia, and the Haemonian rock, or to wooded Geraestus; such was Aeetes, lord of the Colchians, to behold.

Meanwhile, by the instructions of Medea, Jason steeped the charms and sprinkled both his shield and his strong spear, and about them his sword; and his comrades made trial of the weapons, pressing hard, but could not bend that spear even a little, but just so unbroken it held firm in their mighty hands. But Idas, son of Aphareus, raging furiously at them, struck near the butt with his great sword; but the edge leaped back like a hammer from an anvil, rebounding; and they shouted, the heroes, glad in their hopes of the contest. And then he too sprinkled himself; and a dread valour entered him, unspeakable and fearless; and on either side his hands quivered, swelling with strength. And as when a war-horse, eager for battle, neighing prances and beats the ground, while above exulting it lifts its neck with ears erect; such was Aeson's son, exulting in the strength of his limbs. And often this way and that he sprang aloft with bounding step, brandishing in his hands the bronze shield and the ashen spear. You would say that through the dark sky there darted a wintry lightning flash, leaping out frequently from the clouds, when after it they bring the blackest rain. And then not for long were they to hold back from the contests; but seated in order on the benches swiftly they hastened to the plain of Ares. It lay as far in front, on the opposite side of the city, as is the turning-post from the starting-line that a chariot can reach, when for a king who has died his kinsmen set games for foot-racers and horsemen. And they found Aeetes and the throngs of the other Colchians, some standing on the Caucasian crags, and the king himself winding along beside the river's edge.

And Aeson's son, when his comrades had made fast the stern-cables, then with spear and shield went forth to the contest, leaping from the ship; and at once he took the gleaming helmet of bronze, full of sharp teeth, and his sword about his shoulders, his body bare, in part like Ares, in part like Apollo of the golden sword. And glancing over the field he saw the bronze yokes of the bulls, and beside them the plough of one piece of stubborn adamant. Then he came near and fixed his mighty spear, upright on its butt, and laying his helmet against it set it down. And he went forward with his shield alone, tracking the countless footprints of the bulls; and they, from somewhere out of an unseen cavern beneath the earth, where were their strong stalls wrapped about with murky smoke, both came forth together, breathing flame of fire. And the heroes were afraid when they saw them. But he, planting his feet well, withstood them as they came on, as a sea-rock abides the waves driven by countless gusts. And before him he held his shield to face them; and the two with bellowing struck it with their strong horns; yet not a whit did they shift him as they charged. And as when in the perforated melting-pots the bellows of smiths now blaze brightly, kindling the deadly fire, and now cease from their blast, and a dread roar rises from it, whenever it darts up from below; so they, breathing the swift flame from their mouths, roared; and the consuming heat played about him, striking like the lightning-flash; but the girl's charms protected him. And he, seizing the tip of the right bull's horn, dragged it with all his might mightily, to bring it near the bronze yoke, and threw it down on the ground on its knees, swiftly striking with his foot its foot of bronze. So too the other he tripped upon its knees as it charged, smitten with a single blow. And casting wide his broad shield to the ground, on this side and that standing firm, he held both of them fallen upon their fore-knees, dashing straight through the flame. And Aeetes marvelled at the man's strength. And meanwhile the sons of Tyndareus—for so it had long been arranged for them— brought him near the yoke from the ground to cast about them. And he bound their necks well; and lifting up between them the bronze plough-pole, he fitted it to the yoke by its sharp tip. And the two back from the fire to the ship withdrew. But he again, taking up his shield, set it on his back behind, and grasped the helmet full of sharp teeth, and his irresistible spear, with which, like a labourer goading with a Pelasgian prick, he pricked the oxen beneath, stabbing their flanks; and very steadily he guided the well-fitted plough-handle, wrought of adamant. And they for a while raged exceedingly, breathing fierce flame of fire; and their breath rose like the roar of blustering winds, which most of all fearing, seafarers furl their great sail. But not long after, urged on by the spear, they went; and the rugged fallow was broken up behind, cleft by the strength of the bulls and the mighty ploughman. And dreadfully the clods crashed together along the furrows of the plough, breaking, each a man's burden; and he himself followed, pressing the plough-tail down with his stout foot; and far from himself he kept casting the teeth ever along the ploughed clod, glancing back, lest the deadly crop of earthborn men should rise against him first; and they pressed on labouring with their bronze hooves. And when the third part of the waning day is left from dawn, and the weary labourers call for the welcome unyoking-time to come quickly, then the fallow was ploughed by the unwearying ploughman, though it was four acres; and he loosed the ploughs from the oxen. And these he scared off to flee toward the plain; but he himself went back again to the ship, while still he saw the furrows empty of the earthborn men. And about him his comrades heartened him with words. And he from the river's stream drew water in his very helmet and quenched his thirst; and bent his knees, light and supple, and filled his great spirit with valour, raging like a boar, which whets its teeth against the hunting men, and round about much foam drips to the ground from its mouth in its rage. And now over all the field the earthborn were springing up; and the precinct of Ares the destroyer of men bristled with stout shields and double-pointed spears and gleaming helmets; and the gleam reached from below to Olympus, flashing through the air. And as when, after much snow has fallen to the ground, the gusts again scatter the wintry clouds in the murky night, and all together appear the gleaming stars shining through the gloom; so they shone, springing up above the earth. But Jason remembered the counsels of cunning Medea, and seized from the plain a great rounded stone, the dread quoit of Ares Enyalius; not four young men in their prime could have lifted it a little from the earth. This, taking it in his hand, he hurled from afar into their midst, springing up; and he himself crouched beneath his shield, unseen, in confidence. And the Colchians shouted greatly, as when the sea roars, thundering on sharp reefs; and speechless amazement seized Aeetes at the cast of the mighty quoit. And they, like swift hounds leaping about, slew one another with a roar; and upon the earth their mother they fell beneath their own spears, like pines or oaks, which the gusts of wind shake down. And as a fiery star darts from heaven, trailing a furrow of light, a portent to men who behold it flashing through the dark air; such was the son of Aeson as he rushed upon the earthborn, and drew his naked sword from the sheath, and reaped them in confusion, mowing them down, many while still half-risen to the air with belly and flanks; and some reaching up to the shoulders; some newly standing; and some already hurrying on their feet to battle. And as when, at a war stirred up over boundaries, a husbandman, fearing lest his fields be cut down before him, seizing in his hands a curved newly-whetted sickle, hastens and reaps the unripe corn, nor waits for it to dry in season under the rays of the sun; so then he reaped the crop of earthborn men; and with blood the furrows, like the channels of fountains, were filled with streams. And they fell, some biting with their teeth the rough clod prone, some backward, some upon elbow and side, like sea-monsters in form to behold. And many, smitten before they could lift their foot from the earth, as far as they had thrust up into the air, so much to the ground sank down, leaning with their drooping heads. Even so perhaps young shoots, when Zeus has rained unspeakably, newly-reared in a plantation, droop to the ground broken from the root, the labour of garden men; and dejection and deadly grief come upon the planter and lord of the plot; so then upon the lord Aeetes heavy anguish came beneath his heart. And he went back to the city among the Colchians, brooding how most swiftly he might thwart them.
And the day ended, and Jason's contest was accomplished.

Now do you yourself, goddess, tell of the toil and the cunning of the Colchian maiden, Muse, child of Zeus. For truly within me my mind whirls in speechlessness as I ponder whether to call it the love-stricken affliction of madness, or to name it unseemly flight, by which she left the people of the Colchians.

Truly Aeetes, among the men of his people, all the noblest, all night long was devising a sheer treachery against them in his halls, his heart angered without ceasing at the hateful contest; nor did he at all suppose that these things had been accomplished apart from his own daughters.

But Hera cast a most grievous fear into Medea's heart; and she trembled, as a swift fawn, which the baying of hounds has terrified in the thickets of a deep wood. For at once she divined unerringly that she had not hidden her aid, and would soon fulfil all calamity. And she feared her handmaids who were privy to it; and her eyes were filled with fire, and dreadfully her ears rang round. Often she clutched at her throat, and often by the hair she dragged at her locks, moaning in grievous anguish. And there and then the maiden would have perished beyond her doom, swallowing the drugs, and frustrated Hera's purposes, had not the goddess stirred her to flee, dismayed, with the sons of Phrixus; and her fluttering spirit within her grew warm; and turning back she poured out all at once from her bosom all the drugs together into the casket. And she kissed her bed and the folding doors on either side, the door-posts, and she touched the walls; and tearing off a long lock with her hands, she left in the chamber memorials of her maidenhood for her mother, and with a sorrowful voice she lamented: "This long lock I leave you in my stead, as I go, my mother; farewell, even though I go far away; farewell, Chalciope, and all the house. Would that the sea, stranger, had broken you in pieces, before you reached the Colchian land."

So she spoke; and from her eyelids she shed a flood of tears. And as a captive girl, stolen away from a wealthy house, whom newly fate has parted from her country, and who has not yet made trial of grievous toil, but still unused to misery and slavish labours goes dismayed beneath the harsh hands of a mistress; such was the lovely maiden as she rushed from the house. And of themselves the bolts of the doors gave way before her, leaping back at the swift strains of her chant. And with bare feet she ran along the narrow ways, with her left hand drawing her robe over her brow about her forehead and her fair cheeks, and with her right lifting up the hem of her tunic on high. And quickly along the dim path, outside the towers of the spacious city, she came in her fear; nor did any of the watchmen know her; she escaped them as she set out. From there she well purposed to go to the temple; for she was not ignorant of the ways, having often before wandered about the corpses, and about the baneful roots of the earth, as do women who deal in drugs; and her heart throbbed with trembling fear. And the Titanian goddess, the Moon, newly risen from the horizon, seeing her wandering, rejoiced over her greedily, and spoke thus within her mind: "So I am not the only one, then, that steals away to the Latmian cave, nor am I alone aflame for fair Endymion; truly many a time, mindful of my love, I have been driven aside by your crafty chants, that in the dark night you might work your charms at ease, the deeds dear to you. And now you yourself have a share, it seems, in a like madness; some cruel god has given you Jason to be a grievous affliction. Go then, and endure nonetheless, wise though you are, to bear a load of much groaning anguish."

So she spoke; but her feet swiftly bore the hurrying maiden. And gladly she came up onto the banks of the river, gazing across at the gleam of fire which all night long the heroes were kindling in their joy at the contest's end. Then with a sharp clear voice through the gloom from across the water she called the youngest of the sons of Phrixus, Phrontis; and he with his brothers recognized the maiden's voice and that of Aeson's son himself; and in silence the comrades marvelled, when they understood what indeed was the truth. Three times she called; three times, at the urging of the company, Phrontis answered in turn; and meanwhile the heroes rowed toward her with swift oars. Not yet were they casting the ship's cables onto the opposite shore, when Jason set his swift feet on the dry land from on high upon the deck; and after him Phrontis and Argus, the two sons of Phrixus, leaped to the ground; and she, clasping them with both arms about their knees, addressed them: "Save me, friends, wretched as I am, from ruin, and save yourselves likewise from Aeetes; for all is now made plain and open, nor is there any remedy. But let us flee in the ship, before he mounts his swift horses. And I will give the golden fleece, when I have lulled the guardian serpent to sleep; but you, stranger, before your comrades make the gods witnesses of the words you pledged to me; nor, when I have set out far from here, through lack of kinsfolk make me contemptible and shamed."

So she spoke in her distress; and greatly the heart of Aeson's son rejoiced; and at once, as she lay fallen about his knees, he gently raised her up and embraced her, and heartened her: "Strange one, let Zeus himself of Olympus be my witness, and Hera the goddess of marriage, the consort of Zeus, that truly I will set you up as my wedded wife in my halls, when we come back to the land of Hellas."

So he spoke, and at once he joined her right hand with his hand; and she bade them drive the swift ship into the sacred grove at once, that while it was still night they might take and bear away the fleece against the will of Aeetes. And there word and deed were one with their haste. For they put her aboard, and at once thrust the ship from the land; and a great din arose as the chieftains pressed hard at the oars; and she, darting back, stretched out her hands helplessly toward the land. But Jason heartened her with words, and held her in her distress.

At the hour when men cast sleep from their eyes, hunters who, trusting in their dogs, never sleep through the night near to dawn, shunning the light of day, lest it blot out the track of beasts and the scent of the quarry, striking it with its white rays; at that hour Aeson's son and the maiden stepped from the ship upon a grassy spot, which men call the Ram's couch, where it first bent its weary knees, bearing on its back the Minyan son of Athamas. And nearby were the sooty foundations of an altar, which once the Aeolid Phrixus set up to Zeus the protector of fugitives, sacrificing that wholly golden marvel, as Hermes had bidden him, meeting him graciously. There then by the counsels of Argus the chieftains set them down. And the two went along the path into the sacred grove, seeking the huge oak, on which the fleece was cast, like a cloud which at the rising of the sun grows red with his fiery rays. But straight in front the serpent stretched out his long neck, keen-eyed, and seeing them approach with sleepless eyes, and he hissed monstrously; and round about the long banks of the river and the boundless grove resounded. They heard it who, far from Titanian Aea, dwelt in the Colchian land beside the outpourings of Lycus, which, branching off from the loud-roaring river Araxes, joins its sacred stream with Phasis; and the two together, driven into one, pour into the Caucasian sea. And women newly delivered woke in terror, and about their infant children, who were sleeping in their arms, quivering at the hiss, they cast their hands in distress. And as when over smouldering wood the sooty whirls of smoke roll up endlessly, and one ever rises swiftly after another, ever upward from below, soaring aloft in coils; so then that monster writhed his countless spirals, covered with dry scales. And as he writhed, the maiden came before his eyes, calling on Sleep, the helper, highest of the gods, with sweet voice, to charm the monster; and she called upon the queen, the night-wanderer of the underworld, to grant a kindly aid. And Aeson's son followed in fear; but the serpent now, charmed by her song, was relaxing the long ridge of his earthborn coil, and lengthening out his countless circles, as when over the gently rolling deep there rolls a black wave, mute and noiseless; yet even so, lifting his dread head on high, he was eager to enfold them both in his deadly jaws. But she, dipping with a freshly cut sprig of juniper into the brew her pure charms with chants, sprinkled them over his eyes; and all about him the boundless scent of the drug cast sleep; and on the very spot he set down his jaw, resting it; and far behind, the endless coils were stretched out through the deep-rooted wood.

Then Jason took the golden fleece from the oak, at the maiden's bidding; and she, standing firm, smeared the beast's head with the drug, until at last Jason himself bade her turn back to the ship, and he left the shadowy grove of Ares. And as a maiden catches on her fine robe the gleam of the full moon as it rises on high above her chamber-roof; and her heart within rejoices as she gazes on the fair radiance; so then Jason, glad of heart, lifted up the great fleece in his hands; and upon his fair cheeks and his brow there settled, from the shimmering of the wool, a flush like fire. And as great as the hide of a yearling ox or of a stag, which hunters call a brocket, so great was the golden fleece, all over above. It was heavy, thick-covered with wool; and even the ground ever beneath his feet gleamed before him as he went. And he went now with it cast over his left shoulder, hanging from his neck to his feet, and now again he gathered it up and stroked it; for greatly he feared lest some one, of men or gods, should rob him of it by meeting him.

Dawn was spreading over the earth; and they came to the company; and the young men marvelled to see the great fleece gleaming like the lightning of Zeus. And each one rose eager to touch it and to take it in his hands. But Aeson's son restrained the rest, and over it cast a robe newly made; and he set the maiden in the stern, lifting her up, and spoke this word among them all: "No longer now, friends, hold back from returning to our country. For already the task, for the sake of which we endured this grievous voyage, toiling in misery, has been lightly accomplished by the maiden's counsels. Her, willing as she is, I will bring home to be my wedded wife; but do you preserve her, who has been a noble helper to all Achaea and to your own selves. For surely, I think, Aeetes will come with a host to bar our way from the river to the sea. But, half of you, sitting man at oar in turn, row through the ship; and the other half, holding up oxhide shields, a swift defence against the enemy's shafts, guard our homeward way. Now in our hands we hold our children, our dear country, and our aged parents; and on our venture rests Hellas, to win either disgrace or great glory."

So he spoke, and put on his warlike arms; and they shouted with a great cry in their eagerness. And he, drawing his sword from the sheath, cut the stern-cables of the ship. And armed, close to the maiden, beside the steersman Ancaeus, he took his stand; and the ship was urged on by the rowing of the men as they strove eagerly to drive it at once out of the river.

And already to overweening Aeetes and to all the Colchians the love of Medea and her deeds were well known. And they gathered in assembly with their arms; and as many as are the waves of the wintry sea raised up by the wind, or as many leaves fall to the ground from the leafy wood in the month of leaf-fall—who could reckon them? so countless were they that streamed along the banks of the river, shouting in their fury. And Aeetes in his well-wrought chariot shone with his horses, which Helios had given him, swift as the gusts of the wind, lifting in his left hand his rounded shield, and in the other a huge pine-torch; and beside him his spear, mighty, was set straight out before him. And the reins of the horses Apsyrtus held in his hands. But out ahead the ship was already cleaving the sea, urged on by the strong rowers, and by the great river's down-rushing stream.

But the king, lifting his hands in his grievous calamity, called on Helios and Zeus to witness the evil deeds; and dreadfully he cried aloud to all his people, that if they did not bring him his daughter into his own hands, either on the land or finding the ship still afloat on the swell of the sea, and so satisfy his spirit, raging to avenge all these things, they would learn upon their own heads all his wrath, taking upon themselves all his ruin.

So spoke Aeetes; and on that same day the Colchians drew down their ships, and put the tackle aboard them, and on that same day went out upon the sea; nor would you say that this was a fleet of so many ships, but that an endless swarm of birds flocked clamouring over the waters.

And they, with the wind blowing swift by the will of the goddess Hera, that with all speed an evil to the house of Pelias, Aeaean Medea, might reach the Pelasgian land, on the third dawn made fast the ship's cables on the shores of the Paphlagonians, before the river Halys. For she bade them go ashore and propitiate Hecate with sacrifice. And as for all that the maiden made ready in preparing the offering, let no one know of it, nor may my spirit urge me to sing of it. I shrink to tell. Yet the shrine still remains, from that time, which the heroes built to the goddess on the shore, for later-born men to see even to this day.

And at once Aeson's son remembered, and the other heroes too, Phineus, who had said that another voyage would lie before them from Aea; but it was unknown to all alike. And Argus spoke to their longing: "We are going to Orchomenus, which that unerring seer, with whom you met before, charged you to make for. For there is another voyage, which the priests of the immortals pointed out, those who are sprung from Tritonian Thebes. Not yet were all the constellations that wheel in heaven, nor was anything of the sacred race of the Danaans yet to be heard of by inquirers; the Arcadian Apidanians alone existed, the Arcadians, who, men say, lived even before the moon, eating acorns in the hills. Nor was the Pelasgian land then ruled by the glorious Deucalidae, at the time when Eeria, rich in corn, was famed, mother Egypt of the men born in earlier days, and the fair-flowing river Triton, by which all Eeria is watered; for never does rain from Zeus moisten it; but from its outpourings the fields spring up with grain. From there they say a certain man journeyed round through all Europe and Asia, trusting in the might and strength of his peoples and in his own courage; and countless cities he founded as he went, some of which men inhabit perhaps even now, and some not; for much time enough has passed over them. But Aea indeed still remains firm even now, and the descendants of those men whom he settled to dwell in Aea, who indeed keep the writings of their fathers, tablets, on which are all the ways and the bounds of sea and land for those who journey round about. And there is a certain river, the uttermost horn of Ocean, broad and very deep, navigable for a merchant ship; they marked it out far off and named it Ister; which indeed for a while cleaves a boundless plain, flowing alone; for its springs murmur far away beyond the blast of the north wind, in the Rhipaean mountains. But when it reaches the borders of the Thracians and Scythians, there it divides, and one part casts its water here into the eastern sea, and the other part behind flows through a deep gulf, splitting off where it rises up into the Trinacrian sea, which lies along your land, if indeed Achelous truly springs from your land."

So he spoke; and the goddess granted them an auspicious sign, at which all, seeing it, gave a shout of approval to set out on that path. For there appeared before them a trail of heavenly light, where the way was passable. And glad, leaving there the son of Lycus, with sails spread they voyaged over the sea, gazing at the mountains of the Paphlagonians. Nor did they round Carambis, since the breezes and the gleam of the heavenly fire held, until they reached the great stream of Ister.

And of the Colchians some, searching in vain, passed out through the Cyanean rocks of the Pontus; and others again went to the river, those whom Apsyrtus ruled, and turning aside he cut through the Fair Mouth. And so he outstripped them, casting himself over the neck of land into the innermost gulf of the Ionian sea. For there is an island enclosed by Ister, named Peuce, three-cornered, broad toward the shores, but turning a narrow elbow to the stream; and about it the outflow divides in two. One they call Narex; the other, at the lower end, the Fair Mouth. Through this Apsyrtus and the Colchians swiftly set out; but the heroes were sailing high up beyond the topmost end of the island, far away. And in the meadows the shepherds of the field left their countless flocks for fear of the ships, as though they saw beasts coming up out of the monster-teeming sea. For never yet had they seen ships of the sea, neither the Scythians mingled with the Thracians, nor the Sigynni, nor the Graucenii, nor the Sindi who already dwell on the great desolate plain about Laurium. But when they had passed Mount Angurus, and far from Mount Angurus the crag by Cauliacus, about which Ister, splitting his stream this way and that, casts into the sea, and the Laurian plain, then indeed the Colchians, sailing out into the Cronian sea, cut off the ways on every side, lest the heroes escape them. And these came down behind by the river, and passed out near the two Brygean islands of Artemis. In one of these was a sacred shrine; but on the other they landed, avoiding the host of Apsyrtus; for the Colchians had left those islands, out of many, untouched, in reverence for the daughter of Zeus; but the others, thronged with Colchians, blocked the passages of the sea. And likewise he left a host upon the shores near the islands as far as the river Salangon and the Nestian land. There then the Minyae, fewer in number, would have yielded in dread battle to the more numerous; but first they made a covenant, avoiding a great quarrel: the golden fleece, since Aeetes himself had promised it to them, if they should accomplish the contests, that they should hold it justly and in good right, whether by guile or even openly they had taken it from him against his will; but as for Medea—for this was the matter in dispute— to entrust her to the daughter of Leto apart from the company, until some one of the law-bearing kings should decide whether it was right for her to go back to her father's house, or to follow the chieftains to the land of Hellas.

Then, when the maiden had reckoned up each thing in her mind, sharp anguish stirred her heart unceasingly; and at once, drawing Jason alone apart from his comrades, she led him aside, until they had withdrawn far off; and to his face she uttered a sorrowful word: "Aeson's son, what is this plan you have devised together concerning me? Has your good fortune cast you wholly into forgetfulness, and do you give no heed to all that you spoke when you were held fast by need? Where are the oaths of Zeus the suppliants' god, where have your honeyed promises gone? For their sake I, with no fitting modesty, in shameless will, left my country and the glory of my house and my very parents, which were dearest to me; and far away, alone, over the sea, with the doleful halcyons I am borne, for the sake of your labours, that, safe, you might accomplish the contests of the bulls and the earthborn men. And at the last the fleece too, when the matter was made known, you won by my folly; and a baneful shame I poured over womankind. Therefore I declare myself to be your child and wife and sister, as I follow you to the land of Hellas. Now stand by me everywhere with a ready heart, nor leave me alone apart from you, when you go to the kings. But just so defend me; let your justice be firm, and the right, which we both agreed upon; or else strike at once with the sword through the middle of my throat, that I may win the fitting reward for my folly. Wretch that I am, if this king should adjudge me to be my brother's, to whom you are entrusting these grievous covenants—both of them! How shall I come before my father's eyes? With a good name indeed? What vengeance, or what heavy ruin, shall I not endure most bitterly, for the dreadful things I have done? And will you win a homecoming to your heart's content?
